stops.name: Breisacherwald, Feirefiss the black-and-white brother
stops.campa: In the great oak forest north of Istein, a magnificently armed stranger rides ashore from a fleet anchored in a closed arm of the Rhine and challenges Parzival to single combat; the two fight so evenly that the sword Parzival robbed from dead Ither breaks sheer on the heathen's helmet, God no longer willing him lord of a stolen blade, at which the stranger, rather than press it, casts his own weapon far from him, refusing to win against an unarmed knight. Only then do names come out: this is Feirefiss, the black-and-white son Gahmuret left behind, Parzival's half-brother, sailing west in search of the father neither ever really had.
stops.quote: Now I see well, thou gallant hero, thou hast no sword wherewith to fight, and the fame shall be small I win me if I fight with an unarmed knight.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Feirefiss to Parzival

stops.name: The Kembs plain, Cundrie's return and the call to the throne
stops.campa: The morning after the brothers' reconciliation, Cundrie the sorceress rides again into camp, this time not to curse but to kneel: the stars have turned, she says, and named Parzival at last as the destined lord of the Grail, if he will only come now, this Whitsuntide, and ask the question the years have taught him to ask. She names his young son by Condwiramurs, Kardeis, unborn when he left Pelrapeire and unknown to him until this hour, and Loherangrin, a second son, both proof his marriage bore fruit through all the wandering. Parzival chooses Feirefiss to ride with him; Cundrie leads the way.
stops.quote: Now rejoice with a humble heart, since the crown of all earthly blessings henceforward shall be thy part, for read is the mystic writing. The Grail, It doth hail thee king, and Kondwiramur, thy true wife, thou shalt to thy kingdom bring.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XV, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), Cundrie to Parzival

stops.name: Barbigoel to Schönmatt: the ride to Munsalvaesche, and the redemption of Anfortas
stops.campa: On Whitsun Saturday the three ride through Barbigoel, Basle, over Karchobra at Münchenstein, and down by Winterhalde to Schönmatt, until Munsalvaesche rises above them from the Hornikopf as it did that first September evening. In the great round hall, before Anfortas laid dying on his litter, the lance is carried in once more, and this time Parzival, kneeling thrice in the Name of the Trinity, asks the question all Terre de salvaesche has waited a generation to hear: what aileth thee here, mine uncle? Anfortas is healed in an instant; the wound closes; the king of the Grail names his successor with his own breath.
stops.quote: What aileth thee here, mine uncle?
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894), the Grail question

stops.name: Birseck, the night visit to Trevrizent
stops.campa: In the same night of the redemption, before dawn can even announce Whitsunday, Parzival rides down from Munsalvaesche with a company of Templars to the grotto at Birseck to bring Trevrizent the news his own prayers of six Good Fridays have finally answered. The hermit who once told him God's help would never fail weeps to hear it confirmed, and blesses his nephew now not as a penitent but as the Grail King he always half suspected the boy in the fool's coat would become, closing a circle that began the day the two first met in ash and hair shirt.

stops.name: Stollenrain, the dawn reunion with Kyot and Condwiramurs
stops.campa: At the place of the three blood-drops near Dornachbrugg, where six years before a fallen goose's blood on snow first showed him his wife's face, Parzival meets at dawn his uncle Kyot, who has ridden the length of France to bring Condwiramurs and their son Kardeis from Montpellier to the Grail throne, exactly as he once escorted Schoysiane to this same country a generation earlier. The reunion is wordless at first, husband and wife having parted as strangers to what either would become; Kyot, his errand done, turns back toward Montpellier to raise young Kardeis to rule there in his father's stead.

stops.name: Fontane la salvaesche, the death of Sigune
stops.campa: Toward evening, leading his wife and son up toward Munsalvaesche, Parzival halts by the rock arch that has marked every turn of his story, and climbs with them the stairs cut into the cave to greet Sigune a last time. She is dead, still kneeling in the posture of grief she never once set down in six years, Schionatulander's embalmed body still in her lap. They open the tomb and lay her to rest beside him at last, the two lovers united in death as they never were permitted to be in life, while Condwiramurs weeps for a woman she has never met but instantly understands.
stops.quote: There, embalmed lay Schionatulander, nor long should he lie alone, for beside him they laid the maiden, who in life to him true love gave in such wise as beseemed a maiden, and they closed o'er the twain the grave.
stops.quote_source: Wolfram von Eschenbach, Parzival, Book XVI, trans. Jessie L. Weston (1894)

stops.name: Munsalvaesche, Whitsunday: Parzival crowned Grail King
stops.campa: That Whitsuntide evening the whole company of Templeisen receives Condwiramurs as their new queen with a feast at which the Grail mystery play is performed again, not to test a silent guest but to seat him as host. Parzival is enthroned where Anfortas suffered so long, Feirefiss beside him newly baptized for love of Repanse de Schoie, whom he will marry and carry east to found, the story says, a line of Christian kings in his mother's country. The fool who once knelt to armored strangers thinking them gods now sits where the Grail itself once fed four hundred, and is fed by no one's error ever again.
